items.title: Harold Dejan Interview, 1963-03-29
items.q: But Chris Kelly, Punch, Renee, you'd see them maybe every Sunday.

ctx.x: And them bands used to advertise on them trucks.

On the trucks, yeah. They'd like Chris Kelly, Kid Renee, Punch, another good trombone I used to have around here, too. The Albus and I had. But Chris Kelly, Punch, Renee, you'd see them maybe every Sunday. Every Sunday. Every Sunday you could maybe look for them on a truck or a furniture wagon. First, you'd go on a furniture wagon, pulled by a mule or a horse, then later on they'd start going on trucks.
Well, they'd meet up sometime on the corner?

Punch and all that. Oh yeah, like, well, Kid Renier was another one. It was a pleasure. I mean, he was in the top lot. Oh yeah, he was a pleasure. You know, the first time I heard Kid Renier it was really odd. I had been hearing about Kid Renier for years. And when I heard him and I saw him, in fact, he didn't even seem to be a type of man to me. I thought he was a great big fella, the way he used to talk about him, but he was a very small fella. Yes, he got him to take. And when I heard him play, so I asked a…
Oh yeah, I mean, did you hear him when he was in his head there?

items.title: Harold Dejan Interview, 1960-11-18
items.q: when I was playing the gypsy team with Kid Renee

ctx.x: That was the other squad that wasn't the regular police. Yeah, yeah.

Then he was jealous of the boy, changed suits two, three times. Any time he'd go home he'd come out and let a suit and change him and just like, you felt like changing him. And you know how it is, I mean, you get to the point you get jealous of one and wondering why he getting the clothes from. How he's guilty. But everybody was just crazy about him, that's all. Just like a little child. When he'd come in the club and when I was playing the gypsy team with Kid Renee, he'd come in the club, I mean all the girls…
He never made a record I guess except his family may have some acetate probably would be on his track stuff.
